newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela says Irish foes serious about peace.
newsitem.headline: Mandela says Irish foes serious about peace.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela said on Friday that visiting delegations from Northern Ireland's divided political factions were serious about seeking peace in their troubled homeland.

"It is dificult to predict what human beings, what political parties are likely to do in the future. What is significant is that they are here and that alone is a sign that they are serious in searching for peace," Mandela told BBC radio in an interview.

South Africa, a nation still undergoing its own process of reconciliation after decades of racist white rule, has sought a high profile in international peace-making recently, most notably in trying to end the civil war in the former Zaire.

It plans to pass on experience of its own dramatic shift from whites-only rule to democracy to the visitors from Northern Ireland, but will address Sinn Fein republicans and pro-British Ulster Unionists separately, a minister said on Friday.

South African Minister of Constitutional Affairs Mohammed Valli Moosa said nine Northern Ireland political parties would gather at Arniston, east of Cape Town, but would not directly discuss the breakdown in their own peace efforts.
"This is not a continuation or part of negotiations on the Northern Ireland question. It is about discussing the South African transition," he told a news conference.
Mandela also played down what South Africa could do. "Naturally we will give whatever help we can give, which is not unique to South Africa," he said.
Moosa said arrangements were in place to ensure that the Unionists did not have to meet or see the Sinn Fein delegation during the three-day conference.
Valli Moosa was deputy chief negotiator for Mandela's African National Congress (ANC) in constitutional talks with the former white National Party government of F.W. de Klerk.

South Africa's bloody racial conflict largely ended after de Klerk repudiated apartheid in 1990, freed Mandela from prison and legalised his ANC. The country held peaceful elections in 1994 and then spent two years negotiating a permanent post-apartheid constitution that went into force in February.

"They want to know what happened in South Africa. It is a very natural thing for people involved in conflict, especially where there is a possibility for negotiations, to look closely at what happened in South Africa," Valli Moosa said.

He said the Ulster Unionist Party delegation headed by party leader David Trimble and the Democratic Unionist Party team headed by party leader Peter Robinson had sought assurances that they would not see or share a room with Sinn Fein chief negotiator Martin McGuiness's delegation.

An official said the South Africans would brief the nine Irish parties in parallel sessions. "There are two bars and two dining rooms and the South Africans will do every briefing twice so those who don't want to will not even have to see each other in the distance," he said.
The meeting will take place at a high-security complex used under apartheid for the development of a South African missile engine and since then mainly for conferences and sensitive negotiations.
The centre is in the De Hoop nature reserve and less than 10 km (six miles) from the small beach resort of Arniston.

The Irish participants represent the Alliance Party, the Social Democratic Labour Party, the Democratic Unionist Party, the Ulster Democratic Party, the Labour Party, the Ulster Unionist Party, the Progressive Unionist Party, the Women's Coalition and Sinn Fein.
